case: A 71-year-old Black man comes to the physician because of low back pain for 3 months that is worse at night. His father was diagnosed with prostate cancer at age 62, and his sister had breast cancer at age 44. Digital rectal examination shows a hard, irregular nodule in the left lobe of the prostate. Serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is 48 ng/mL (less than 4.0), alkaline phosphatase is 310 U/L (40 to 130), and calcium is 9.6 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5). Radiographs show sclerotic lesions in the L3 and L4 vertebral bodies and both iliac bones. Needle biopsy shows infiltrating small glands lined by a single layer of cells with prominent nucleoli. Diagnosis: prostate adenocarcinoma with bone metastases.

questions.stem: The pathologist reports a Gleason score of 4 + 4 = 8. Which of the following features of the tumor is the basis of this score?
options: Degree of nuclear pleomorphism and nucleolar size
Number of mitotic figures per high-power field
Architectural pattern of the malignant glands
Depth of invasion through the prostatic capsule
approach: Recall that most tumor grades rest on nuclear features or mitoses, and prostate cancer is the classic exception.
Gleason grading looks at gland architecture at low power: well-formed glands (pattern 3), fused or cribriform glands (pattern 4), and sheets or single cells (pattern 5).
The two most common patterns are added to give the score.
questions.why: Gleason grading is based only on the architectural pattern of the tumor glands seen at low magnification. Each pattern gets a number, and the most common and second most common patterns are added together. Pattern 4 means fused, poorly formed, or cribriform glands, so a score of 8 is high grade. That fits a tumor that has already reached bone. Grade is separate from stage, which describes how far the tumor has spread.
whyNot: Nuclear pleomorphism is the basis of nuclear grading in other carcinomas, such as breast cancer. Prostate cancer nuclei are often fairly uniform, so the Gleason system does not use nuclear detail.
Mitotic count is part of grading for breast carcinoma and for sarcomas. It is not part of the Gleason system.
Correct.
Extension through the capsule is a feature of stage (the T category), not grade.

questions.stem: A bone scan shows multiple lesions in the lumbar vertebrae and pelvis, and CT of the chest shows no lung nodules. Which of the following best explains how tumor cells reached the lumbar spine without first lodging in the lungs?
options: Flow through the valveless vertebral venous plexus
Lymphatic spread through the para-aortic lymph nodes
Arterial spread through the lumbar segmental arteries
Portal venous drainage through the inferior mesenteric vein
approach: Notice the pattern: lumbar spine and pelvis involved, lungs spared.
Blood from the prostatic venous plexus normally drains to the internal iliac veins and then through the lungs.
The valveless vertebral venous plexus (Batson plexus) links the prostatic and pelvic veins directly to the vertebral bodies, bypassing the lungs.
questions.why: The prostatic venous plexus connects with the vertebral venous plexus, a network of valveless veins around the spine. When abdominal pressure rises, as with coughing or straining, blood can flow backward from the pelvis into these veins and carry tumor cells straight to the lumbar vertebrae and pelvis. This route skips the lung capillary filter. Prostate cancer cells in bone then stimulate osteoblasts, which produce sclerotic lesions, bone pain, and a high serum alkaline phosphatase, as in this patient.
whyNot: Correct.

Prostate cancer does spread to pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes, but lymph returns to the venous blood through the thoracic duct and then passes through the lungs. Nodal spread does not give a direct route to the vertebral bodies.
Tumor cells that enter the systemic veins must pass through the pulmonary capillaries before they can reach any systemic artery, so arterial spread would usually leave lung lesions first.
The inferior mesenteric vein drains the left colon into the portal system, which carries tumor cells to the liver. This is a route for colorectal cancer, not prostate cancer.

questions.stem: The nodule was easily felt on digital rectal examination, and he had no urinary hesitancy or weak stream. Which of the following regions of the prostate is the most likely site of origin of this tumor?
options: Anterior fibromuscular stroma
Central zone
Transition zone
Peripheral zone
approach: Combine the clues: a hard nodule felt through the rectal wall and no obstructive urinary symptoms.
The peripheral zone lies posterior and lateral, against the rectum and away from the urethra.
Benign prostatic hyperplasia arises in the transition zone around the urethra, which is why it causes obstructive symptoms early.
questions.why: About 70% of prostate carcinomas arise in the peripheral zone, which forms most of the posterior and lateral gland. This zone lies against the rectum, so tumors there are often felt as hard nodules on rectal examination. Because the peripheral zone is away from the prostatic urethra, these tumors seldom cause early obstructive symptoms. Benign prostatic hyperplasia arises in the transition zone, which surrounds the proximal prostatic urethra.
whyNot: The anterior fibromuscular stroma is mostly smooth muscle and fibrous tissue with few glands, and it faces away from the rectum. Carcinoma rarely starts here.
The central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts at the base of the gland. Only a small share of carcinomas start here.
The transition zone surrounds the urethra and is the site of benign prostatic hyperplasia. Enlargement here compresses the urethra and causes hesitancy and a weak stream early.
Correct.

questions.stem: Because of his sister's early breast cancer and his own diagnosis, germline testing is performed and shows a pathogenic BRCA2 variant. The normal protein product of this gene is required for which of the following DNA repair processes?
options: Base excision repair of deaminated or oxidized bases
Homologous recombination at double-strand breaks
Mismatch repair of errors left after replication
Nucleotide excision repair of bulky DNA adducts
approach: Link the family pattern (prostate cancer and early breast cancer) to hereditary BRCA2 mutation.
Recall that BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressor genes in homologous recombination repair.
A cell loses repair only after a second hit in the normal allele, so inheritance is autosomal dominant while the cell defect is recessive.
questions.why: BRCA2 loads RAD51 onto single-stranded DNA so that a broken strand can copy the matching sequence on the sister chromatid. This is homologous recombination, the error-free repair of double-strand breaks. Carriers inherit one faulty copy in an autosomal dominant pattern. After a second, somatic hit, cells must use error-prone repair, and mutations build up. BRCA2 carriers have a higher risk of breast and ovarian cancer and, in men, of breast and prostate cancer, which fits this family.
whyNot: Base excision repair uses glycosylases to remove single damaged bases, such as uracil formed by cytosine deamination. It is not the BRCA2 pathway.
Correct.
Mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) are defective in Lynch syndrome, which raises the risk of colon and endometrial cancer.
Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers. Its defect causes xeroderma pigmentosum and skin cancers.

dx: Ovarian torsion from a mature cystic teratoma, with a paraovarian cyst as the differential
case: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of sudden, severe right lower quadrant pain that began 4 hours ago during exercise, with nausea and two episodes of vomiting. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Pelvic ultrasound shows an enlarged right ovary containing a 7-cm cystic mass with echogenic fat and a focus of calcification, and Doppler shows reduced flow to the ovary. The differential diagnosis includes a twisted paraovarian cyst. At laparoscopy, the right adnexa is twisted twice on its pedicle. The ovary is untwisted and the cyst is removed; it contains sebaceous material, hair, and a tooth. Diagnosis: ovarian torsion caused by a mature cystic teratoma.

questions.stem: At laparoscopy, the twisted ovary is enlarged, edematous, and dark blue-black, but it turns pink within minutes of being untwisted. Which of the following best explains these findings?
options: Immediate arterial occlusion with pale coagulative infarction
Cyst rupture with chemical peritonitis and serosal edema
Hemorrhage from a corpus luteum into the ovarian stroma
Venous outflow blocked first, with arterial inflow preserved
approach: Notice the color: a dark, swollen ovary means blood is trapped in it, not simply cut off.
Thin-walled, low-pressure veins collapse under twisting before thick-walled arteries do.
Arteries keep filling a congested ovary until tissue pressure stops them, so prompt untwisting can save it.
questions.why: When the ovary twists on its ligaments, the thin-walled, low-pressure veins collapse first. Arteries keep pumping blood in, so the ovary becomes engorged, edematous, and dark from hemorrhagic congestion. If the twist persists, rising tissue pressure finally stops arterial inflow and the ovary infarcts. Here the ovary turned pink after untwisting, which shows the arterial supply was still working. An ovary enlarged by a cyst or tumor, like this teratoma, is the usual setup for torsion.
whyNot: Pure arterial occlusion gives a pale infarct with no time for congestion. Torsion squeezes the low-pressure veins first, so the ovary turns dark before it infarcts.
Rupture of a teratoma can spill sebaceous material and cause chemical peritonitis, but this cyst was intact and twisted. Rupture would not explain a dark ovary that recovers after untwisting.
Bleeding into a corpus luteum cyst can cause sudden pain, but this ovary held a teratoma and was twisted on its pedicle.
Correct.

questions.stem: Histologic examination of the cyst shows skin with hair follicles and sebaceous glands, cartilage, and respiratory epithelium. If the tumor had instead been composed almost entirely of mature thyroid follicles, which of the following would most likely have been found before surgery?
options: Raised serum alpha-fetoprotein
Suppressed TSH with raised free thyroxine
Raised serum lactate dehydrogenase
Raised serum testosterone with hirsutism and clitoromegaly
approach: Recognize mature tissues from all three germ layers: a mature cystic teratoma.
A teratoma made mostly of thyroid tissue is struma ovarii, a monodermal teratoma.
Functioning thyroid tissue can make hormone on its own, and the high T4 suppresses pituitary TSH.
questions.why: Mature cystic teratoma is the most common ovarian germ cell tumor and contains mature tissues from ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Struma ovarii is a teratoma made mostly of thyroid tissue. That tissue can secrete thyroid hormone outside normal control, causing hyperthyroidism with a high free T4 and, through negative feedback on the pituitary, a suppressed TSH. Removing the tumor cures the hyperthyroidism.
whyNot: Alpha-fetoprotein is raised in yolk sac tumor, a malignant germ cell tumor with Schiller-Duval bodies. Mature thyroid tissue does not make AFP.
Correct.
Lactate dehydrogenase is the marker for dysgerminoma, which is made of sheets of large clear cells. It is not a feature of struma ovarii.
Testosterone excess with virilization points to a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, a sex cord-stromal tumor, not a teratoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following laparoscopic findings would have favored torsion of a paraovarian cyst over torsion of an ovarian mass?
options: Thin-walled cyst in the broad ligament beside a normal ovary
Hemorrhagic cyst within the ovary lined by luteinized cells
Bilateral multiloculated ovarian cysts filled with clear fluid
Ovary studded with cysts of dark brown, chocolate-like fluid
approach: Recall where paraovarian cysts arise: remnants of the Mullerian or Wolffian (mesonephric) ducts in the broad ligament.
The key feature is a cyst separate from the ovary, which looks normal.
The other choices are all cysts inside the ovary itself.
questions.why: Paraovarian cysts are thin-walled, fluid-filled cysts in the broad ligament, between the ovary and the uterine tube. They arise from embryonic remnants of the paramesonephric (Mullerian) or mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts. Because they sit apart from the ovary, the ovary itself looks normal at surgery. Like ovarian masses, a large paraovarian cyst can twist or rupture and cause acute pelvic pain.
whyNot: Correct.
A hemorrhagic cyst lined by luteinized cells is a corpus luteum cyst inside the ovary. It can rupture and bleed into the peritoneum.
Bilateral multiloculated ovarian cysts are theca lutein cysts, which form under very high hCG, as in molar pregnancy. Her pregnancy test was negative.
Ovarian cysts with chocolate-colored fluid are endometriomas from endometriosis. They lie within the ovary, not beside it.

questions.stem: The twisted pedicle compressed the main artery and vein of the right ovary. In which of the following structures do these vessels reach the ovary?
options: Transverse cervical (cardinal) ligament
Round ligament of the uterus
Suspensory ligament of the ovary
Proper ligament of the ovary
approach: Recall that the ovarian artery comes directly from the abdominal aorta and descends to the pelvic brim.
It enters the pelvis inside the suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament, with the ovarian vein and lymphatics.
Torsion twists the adnexa around this ligament and the ovarian ligament, kinking these vessels.
questions.why: The ovarian artery arises from the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries and reaches the ovary through the suspensory ligament of the ovary, also called the infundibulopelvic ligament. The ovarian vein and lymphatics run with it. In torsion, the adnexa rotate around this ligament and the ovarian ligament, so these vessels are kinked. Surgeons also clamp the suspensory ligament when they remove an ovary.
whyNot: The cardinal (transverse cervical) ligament carries the uterine artery and vein at the base of the broad ligament, near the cervix.
The round ligament runs from the uterine horn through the inguinal canal to the labium majus. It carries only a small artery and is not the ovarian supply.
Correct.

The proper ovarian ligament joins the ovary to the uterus. The ovarian branch of the uterine artery runs nearby and joins the ovarian artery, but the main ovarian vessels arrive through the suspensory ligament.

topics: Ligaments of the uterus and ovary

dx: High-grade serous carcinoma of the ovary
case: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because of abdominal bloating, early satiety, and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss over 3 months. Her mother had breast cancer at age 46. Physical examination shows shifting dullness and bilateral adnexal masses. Serum CA-125 is 840 U/mL (less than 35). CT shows ascites, bilateral solid and cystic adnexal masses, and a thickened, nodular omentum. At surgery, both ovaries have surface papillary growths, and tumor nodules cover the omentum and peritoneum. Histologic examination shows papillae and slit-like spaces lined by highly atypical cells with frequent mitoses and scattered laminated calcifications (psammoma bodies). Diagnosis: high-grade serous carcinoma of the ovary.

questions.stem: Sequencing of tumor DNA is performed. A mutation in which of the following genes is most likely to be found?
options: ARID1A
TP53
KRAS
CTNNB1
approach: Identify the subtype: high-grade serous carcinoma, the most common and most lethal ovarian cancer.
Recall that high-grade serous carcinoma carries TP53 mutations in nearly every case, and many also have BRCA1 or BRCA2 loss.
Match the other genes to other ovarian subtypes.
questions.why: Almost all high-grade serous carcinomas carry TP53 mutations, which appear early, even in the precursor lesion. Many of these tumors are now thought to begin in the fimbria of the uterine tube as serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma and then seed the ovary and peritoneum. Women with germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations, such as those with a family history like this patient's, have a much higher risk. Psammoma bodies, a high CA-125, ascites, and omental spread complete the classic picture.
whyNot: ARID1A loss is typical of clear cell and endometrioid carcinomas, which are often linked to endometriosis.
Correct.
KRAS mutations are typical of low-grade serous and mucinous tumors, which grow slowly from borderline precursors.
CTNNB1 (beta-catenin) mutations are typical of endometrioid carcinoma of the ovary.

questions.stem: Which of the following ovarian tumors arises from the same category of cells as this patient's tumor?
options: Dysgerminoma
Granulosa cell tumor
Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor
Brenner tumor
approach: Classify the patient's tumor: serous carcinoma is a surface epithelial tumor.
List the surface epithelial group: serous, mucinous, endometrioid, clear cell, and Brenner (transitional cell).
Sort the remaining choices into germ cell and sex cord-stromal tumors.
questions.why: Ovarian tumors are grouped by the cells they come from. Surface epithelial tumors are the largest group and include most ovarian cancers in older women: serous, mucinous, endometrioid, clear cell, and Brenner tumors. Brenner tumors contain nests of transitional (urothelial-like) cells in a fibrous stroma and are usually benign. Germ cell tumors are most common in young women, and sex cord-stromal tumors often make hormones.
whyNot: Dysgerminoma is a germ cell tumor, the ovarian counterpart of testicular seminoma.
Granulosa cell tumor is a sex cord-stromal tumor that often makes estrogen.
Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor is a sex cord-stromal tumor that often makes androgens.
Correct.

questions.stem: Before surgery, metastatic disease to both ovaries was considered. If an ovarian biopsy had instead shown cellular stroma infiltrated by mucin-filled cells with nuclei pushed to one side, the primary tumor would most likely have been in which of the following organs?
options: Endometrium
Kidney
Stomach
Urinary bladder
approach: Recognize signet ring cells: mucin pushes the nucleus to the edge of the cell.
Signet ring cells in both ovaries define a Krukenberg tumor.
The classic primary is diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma.
questions.why: A Krukenberg tumor is a metastasis to the ovaries, usually both, made of mucin-filled signet ring cells within a reactive, cellular ovarian stroma. The most common primary is diffuse-type adenocarcinoma of the stomach, followed by other gastrointestinal sites such as the colon and appendix. Bilateral ovarian masses should always raise the question of a metastasis. Finding one should prompt a search for the primary tumor.
whyNot: Endometrial carcinoma can spread to the ovaries, but it forms glands, not signet ring cells.
Renal cell carcinoma is made of clear cells full of glycogen and lipid, not mucin, and it rarely spreads to the ovary.
Correct.
Bladder carcinoma is a urothelial tumor and a rare source of ovarian metastasis. It is not a classic source of signet ring cell metastases.

questions.stem: Postoperative CT shows thrombus in the left ovarian vein extending to the point where this vein drains. Into which of the following vessels does the thrombus most likely extend?
options: Left renal vein
Inferior vena cava
Left common iliac vein
Left internal iliac vein
approach: Recall that the gonadal veins drain differently on the two sides.
The right ovarian vein enters the inferior vena cava directly; the left enters the left renal vein at a right angle.
A left ovarian vein thrombus therefore extends into the left renal vein.
questions.why: The ovarian arteries arise from the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries. The right ovarian vein drains straight into the inferior vena cava, but the left ovarian vein drains into the left renal vein. The same pattern in men explains why varicocele is more common on the left: the left testicular vein is longer, joins the renal vein at a right angle, and can be compressed where the left renal vein passes between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery.
whyNot: Correct.
The right ovarian vein drains into the inferior vena cava. The left one drains into the left renal vein.
The common iliac veins drain the pelvis and legs. The ovarian veins run up past them to the renal level.
The internal iliac vein drains the uterus, bladder, and rectum. The ovarian vein leaves the pelvis in the suspensory ligament and does not join it.

dx: Complete hydatidiform mole with theca lutein cysts
case: A 24-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 13 weeks' gestation by dates comes to the physician because of intermittent vaginal bleeding and severe nausea and vomiting for 2 weeks. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 154/100 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a uterus enlarged to the level of the umbilicus, consistent with about 20 weeks' gestation. No fetal heart tones are heard. Urinalysis shows 2+ protein. Serum beta-hCG is 480,000 mIU/mL, far above the range expected at 13 weeks. Ultrasound shows a uterus filled with a heterogeneous mass containing many small cystic spaces, no fetus, and bilateral multiloculated ovarian cysts 7 and 8 cm in diameter. Suction evacuation yields diffusely swollen villi with circumferential trophoblast proliferation. Diagnosis: complete hydatidiform mole with theca lutein cysts.

questions.stem: The karyotype of the molar tissue is 46,XX, and immunostaining for p57 is absent in the villous cytotrophoblast. Which of the following best explains the absent p57 staining?
options: Absence of any maternal chromosomes
Triploidy with one maternal haploid set
Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 11
Somatic deletion of the p57 gene in trophoblast
approach: Recall that p57 (CDKN1C) is paternally imprinted, so only the maternal copy is expressed.
A complete mole forms when an ovum with no maternal nucleus is fertilized, usually by one sperm that duplicates to give 46,XX.
With no maternal genome, no active p57 gene exists, so the stain is negative.
questions.why: In a complete mole, an ovum that has lost its own nucleus is fertilized, most often by one sperm that duplicates its DNA. The result is a 46,XX genome that is entirely paternal. The p57 gene is imprinted: the paternal copy is silenced and only the maternal copy is expressed. With no maternal chromosomes, the villous cytotrophoblast and stroma cannot make p57. A partial mole is triploid with one maternal set, so it stains positive, which is how pathologists tell the two apart.
whyNot: Correct.
A triploid conceptus with one maternal set is a partial mole. The maternal copy of p57 is present, so its cells stain positive.
Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 11 gives two maternal copies of the region, which would increase p57 expression.
Molar trophoblast does not lose p57 by deletion. The absent stain reflects the missing maternal genome, which also fits the all-paternal 46,XX karyotype.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the hypertension and proteinuria in this patient at 13 weeks' gestation?
options: Essential hypertension present before this pregnancy
Thyrotoxicosis from hCG stimulation of the thyroid gland
Early preeclampsia driven by excess abnormal trophoblast
Immune complex glomerulonephritis triggered by pregnancy
approach: Note the timing: preeclampsia normally appears after 20 weeks.
Hypertension with proteinuria before 20 weeks should suggest a molar pregnancy.
The large mass of abnormal trophoblast drives the same endothelial injury as typical preeclampsia, only earlier.
questions.why: Preeclampsia is new hypertension with proteinuria or organ damage after 20 weeks. When it appears earlier, a hydatidiform mole is the classic cause. The mole's large mass of abnormal trophoblast releases antiangiogenic factors such as soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1), which injure the maternal endothelium. This patient also has the other classic findings of a complete mole: bleeding, a uterus large for dates, very high hCG, hyperemesis, and theca lutein cysts.
whyNot: Chronic hypertension would be present before pregnancy, and it would not explain new proteinuria arising with a molar pregnancy.
Very high hCG can stimulate the thyroid and raise systolic pressure, but hyperthyroidism does not cause proteinuria.
Correct.
Glomerulonephritis usually shows hematuria and red cell casts, and pregnancy is not a trigger for it. The molar pregnancy explains her findings.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the ovarian cysts seen on ultrasound?
options: Failure of a dominant follicle to rupture at ovulation
Luteinization of theca cells stimulated by excess hCG
Hemorrhage into a persistent corpus luteum
Endometrial tissue implanted on the ovarian surface
approach: Notice the pattern: large, bilateral, multiloculated cysts with very high hCG.
hCG is structurally similar to LH and acts on LH receptors on theca cells.
Overstimulation makes the theca cells luteinize and the follicles fill with fluid.
questions.why: Theca lutein cysts form when very high hCG, from a mole, choriocarcinoma, or multiple pregnancy, acts on LH receptors in both ovaries. The theca cells luteinize and the follicles swell into many fluid-filled cysts. Because they depend on hCG, the cysts shrink over weeks to months after the mole is evacuated and hCG falls. They can occasionally twist or rupture.
whyNot: A follicle that fails to rupture forms a follicular cyst, which is usually single and one-sided and may make estrogen.
Correct.
Bleeding into a corpus luteum gives a single cyst that can rupture into the peritoneum. It does not give bilateral multiloculated cysts.
Endometrial tissue on the ovary forms an endometrioma filled with old blood (a chocolate cyst), linked to cyclic pain, not to high hCG.

questions.stem: A partial mole, in contrast, usually forms when two sperm fertilize a single ovum. Which of the following events normally prevents a second sperm from fertilizing the ovum?
options: Acrosomal enzyme release that digests the corona radiata
Capacitation of sperm in the female reproductive tract
Completion of the second meiotic division of the oocyte
Cortical granule release that alters the zona pellucida
approach: Identify the problem in a partial mole: two sperm entered one ovum (dispermy).
Recall the block to polyspermy that follows fusion of the first sperm with the oocyte.
A calcium wave makes cortical granules empty their enzymes, which changes the zona pellucida.
questions.why: Fertilization usually takes place in the ampulla of the uterine tube. When the first sperm fuses with the oocyte membrane, a wave of calcium release triggers the cortical reaction. Cortical granules release enzymes that modify zona pellucida proteins, so no other sperm can bind or pass through. The same calcium signal prompts the oocyte to finish its second meiotic division and release the second polar body. If this block fails and two sperm enter, the result is a triploid conceptus such as a partial mole.
whyNot: The acrosome reaction releases enzymes that help a sperm get through the corona radiata and zona pellucida. It helps fertilization and does not block extra sperm.
Capacitation in the female tract prepares sperm for the acrosome reaction. It happens before fertilization and does not prevent polyspermy.
Completion of meiosis II is triggered by sperm entry and forms the female pronucleus. It does not stop other sperm from entering.
Correct.

dx: Gestational choriocarcinoma after an invasive mole
case: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician because of cough with blood-streaked sputum for 2 weeks. Five months ago, she had suction evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole. Her serum beta-hCG fell at first and then plateaued, and pelvic imaging 2 months ago showed molar tissue within the myometrium, but she did not return for treatment. She also reports palpitations and heat intolerance. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 132/76 mm Hg. A 2-cm dark red nodule is seen in the anterior vaginal wall. Serum beta-hCG is 260,000 mIU/mL (less than 5 in nonpregnant women). Chest CT shows multiple nodules in both lungs. Uterine curettage yields hemorrhagic, necrotic tissue with sheets of atypical cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast and no chorionic villi. Diagnosis: gestational choriocarcinoma after an invasive mole.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the early appearance of lung metastases in this patient?
options: Lymphatic spread to pelvic and para-aortic nodes
Transcoelomic seeding across the peritoneal cavity
Vascular invasion by malignant trophoblast
Retrograde venous flow through the vertebral plexus
approach: Recall normal trophoblast behavior: it invades maternal spiral arteries to build the placenta.
Malignant trophoblast keeps this ability, so it enters the blood very early.
Uterine venous blood reaches the lungs first, so lung metastases are most common, followed by the vagina, brain, and liver.
questions.why: Gestational choriocarcinoma is a malignant tumor of cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast with no chorionic villi. Like normal trophoblast, it invades blood vessels, so it spreads through the blood early, often while the uterine tumor is still small. Venous blood from the uterus reaches the lungs first, which is why lung nodules and hemoptysis are common at presentation. Metastases to the vagina, brain, and liver follow, and they bleed easily. The tumor can follow a mole, a miscarriage, an ectopic pregnancy, or a normal pregnancy, and it secretes very high hCG.
whyNot: Lymphatic spread is the usual early route of carcinomas, such as cervical cancer. Choriocarcinoma spreads mainly through the blood.
Transcoelomic seeding across the peritoneum is the typical route of ovarian surface epithelial carcinoma. It does not explain lung nodules.
Correct.
Retrograde flow through the valveless vertebral venous plexus carries prostate cancer to the spine. It does not explain lung metastases.

questions.stem: Two months before this visit, imaging showed molar tissue within the myometrium. Which of the following histologic findings most likely characterized that earlier lesion?
options: Intermediate trophoblast forming a mass at the placental site
Sheets of trophoblast without villi invading the myometrium
Swollen villi confined to the endometrial cavity
Hydropic villi penetrating into the myometrium
approach: Recall what a plateau in hCG after evacuation means: molar tissue has persisted or invaded.
Molar tissue in the myometrium means the swollen villi have grown into the uterine wall, which defines an invasive mole.
Villi are still present, which separates invasive mole from choriocarcinoma.
questions.why: An invasive mole is a mole whose hydropic villi grow into the myometrium and sometimes into its blood vessels. It can perforate the uterus and cause hemorrhage, and it keeps hCG elevated after evacuation. Chorionic villi are still present, which separates an invasive mole from choriocarcinoma, where only sheets of malignant trophoblast are seen, as in this patient's current lesion.
whyNot: A mass of intermediate trophoblast at the implantation site is a placental site trophoblastic tumor. It makes only modest amounts of hCG and makes human placental lactogen.
Sheets of malignant trophoblast without villi describe choriocarcinoma, the lesion she has now.
Swollen villi limited to the endometrial cavity describe the original complete mole, before it invaded the uterine wall.
Correct.

questions.stem: The thyroid gland is not enlarged and has no nodules. Serum TSH is 0.05 μU/mL (0.4 to 4.0), free thyroxine is 3.1 ng/dL (0.8 to 1.8), and thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins are absent. Which of the following best explains her thyroid findings?
options: Activation of TSH receptors by structurally similar hCG
Release of stored hormone from a destructive thyroiditis
Increased thyroxine-binding globulin from high estrogen
Autonomous hormone production by a toxic thyroid nodule
approach: Read the labs: suppressed TSH with high free T4 means primary hyperthyroidism.
With no stimulating antibodies, no nodule, and very high hCG, think of hCG acting on the thyroid.
hCG, LH, FSH, and TSH share an alpha subunit, and hCG is similar enough to TSH to activate the TSH receptor at high levels.
questions.why: hCG, LH, FSH, and TSH are glycoprotein hormones with a common alpha subunit and a hormone-specific beta subunit. hCG is similar enough to TSH that, at very high levels, it binds and activates the TSH receptor on thyroid follicular cells. Gestational trophoblastic disease can produce hCG levels high enough to cause clinical hyperthyroidism, and the high T4 then suppresses pituitary TSH. The hyperthyroidism resolves as hCG falls with treatment.
whyNot: Correct.
Destructive thyroiditis releases stored hormone for a few weeks, but it has no link to a very high hCG, which explains her findings directly.
High estrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin and total T4, but free T4 and TSH stay normal.
A toxic nodule can cause this lab pattern, but her gland has no nodules, and her very high hCG accounts for the thyroid stimulation.

questions.stem: Because this tumor arose from a complete mole, its cells carry only paternal chromosomes and are fully foreign to the mother. Which of the following properties of trophoblast normally limits attack by maternal T cells and natural killer cells?
options: Loss of all HLA class I molecules from the cell surface
Expression of HLA-G in place of HLA-A and HLA-B
High expression of HLA class II molecules
Secretion of IgG that blocks maternal T cell receptors
approach: Recall that cells lacking class I MHC are killed by NK cells (the missing-self response).
Trophoblast avoids T cell attack by not displaying the highly polymorphic HLA-A and HLA-B molecules.
It avoids NK cell attack by displaying HLA-G, a nonclassical class I molecule that engages inhibitory NK receptors.
questions.why: The fetus carries paternal antigens, so it is semiallogeneic to the mother. Trophoblast does not express the highly polymorphic HLA-A and HLA-B molecules or class II molecules, so maternal T cells have little foreign HLA to recognize. It does express HLA-G, a nonclassical class I molecule with very little variation between people. HLA-G binds inhibitory receptors on uterine NK cells and prevents the missing-self response that would otherwise kill a cell lacking class I.
whyNot: Cells that lose all class I molecules become targets for NK cells, which kill cells missing self. Trophoblast avoids this by keeping HLA-G.
Correct.
Class II molecules present antigen to CD4 T cells and would increase recognition. Trophoblast lacks class II.
Trophoblast does not make antibodies. Only plasma cells secrete immunoglobulin.

dx: Gestational diabetes with polyhydramnios and fetal macrosomia
case: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 32 weeks' gestation comes for a prenatal visit. Her hemoglobin A1c at 8 weeks was 5.2% (less than 5.7). At 26 weeks, a 50-g glucose challenge test and a follow-up 100-g oral glucose tolerance test were abnormal, and gestational diabetes was diagnosed. She has had difficulty following her diet. Fasting plasma glucose today is 118 mg/dL (target less than 95 in pregnancy). Fundal height is 38 cm (expected about 32 cm). Ultrasound shows an estimated fetal weight above the 97th percentile, a large fetal abdominal circumference, normal fetal anatomy, and an amniotic fluid index of 29 cm (about 5 to 24). Diagnosis: gestational diabetes with polyhydramnios and fetal macrosomia.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the fetal overgrowth?
options: Transfer of maternal insulin across the placenta to the fetus
Fetal insulin secreted in response to maternal glucose
Human placental lactogen acting directly on fetal tissue
Fetal growth hormone excess from pituitary stimulation
approach: Recall what crosses the placenta: glucose does, by facilitated diffusion through GLUT1, and maternal insulin does not.
High maternal glucose means high fetal glucose, so the fetal pancreas makes more insulin.
Insulin is a major fetal growth hormone, so fat and organ mass increase.
questions.why: Glucose crosses the placenta by facilitated diffusion down its concentration gradient, so fetal glucose follows maternal glucose. Maternal insulin is too large to cross. The fetal beta cells, active from about the end of the first trimester, respond to the high glucose with hyperplasia and high insulin output. Fetal insulin acts as an anabolic growth factor, increasing fat, liver, and heart mass and causing macrosomia. After birth, the maternal glucose supply stops while insulin stays high, so the newborn is at risk of hypoglycemia.
whyNot: Maternal insulin does not cross the placenta in meaningful amounts. Fetal insulin comes only from the fetal pancreas.
Correct.
Human placental lactogen acts on the mother, raising her insulin resistance and so her glucose. It does not drive fetal growth directly.
Fetal growth in late pregnancy depends mainly on insulin and insulin-like growth factors. Pituitary growth hormone plays a minor role.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the increased amniotic fluid volume?
options: Fetal osmotic diuresis that increases urine output
Impaired fetal swallowing from esophageal atresia
Reduced fetal urine output from renal agenesis
Transudation across the amnion from maternal edema
approach: Recall the balance: fetal urine adds amniotic fluid, and fetal swallowing removes it.
Fetal hyperglycemia exceeds renal tubular reabsorption, so glucose pulls water into the urine.
More fetal urine means more amniotic fluid; the normal anatomy scan argues against a swallowing defect.
questions.why: In the second half of pregnancy, most amniotic fluid is fetal urine, and fetal swallowing removes it. When the fetus is hyperglycemic, glucose spills into the urine and causes an osmotic diuresis, so fluid builds up. Polyhydramnios also follows anything that prevents swallowing, such as esophageal atresia or anencephaly, but this fetus has normal anatomy. Oligohydramnios is the opposite pattern and comes from low urine output, as in bilateral renal agenesis.
whyNot: Correct.
Esophageal atresia causes polyhydramnios because the fetus cannot swallow fluid, but the ultrasound showed normal anatomy, and maternal diabetes explains the finding.
Renal agenesis stops fetal urine production and causes oligohydramnios with Potter sequence, the opposite of this finding.
Maternal edema does not move fluid into the amniotic cavity. Amniotic volume depends mainly on fetal urine and swallowing.

questions.stem: Infants of mothers with poorly controlled diabetes before conception have higher rates of congenital heart defects and caudal regression. Which of the following best explains why this patient's fetus does not share that higher risk of major malformations?
options: Placental glucose transport begins only after 20 weeks
The embryonic pancreas buffers glucose during weeks 3 to 8
Maternal insulin protects the embryo early in gestation
Her hyperglycemia began after organogenesis was complete
approach: Use her early A1c: it was normal at 8 weeks, so her glucose was normal during early development.
Recall that organs form in the embryonic period, weeks 3 to 8 after fertilization.
Gestational diabetes appears in the second half of pregnancy, after organogenesis, so it affects growth more than structure.
questions.why: The embryonic period runs from gastrulation in week 3, when the trilaminar disc forms, to the end of week 8, when the organ primordia have been laid down. Teratogens act most strongly in this window because a disruption can derail a whole organ system. Maternal hyperglycemia during these weeks, as in poorly controlled pregestational diabetes, raises the risk of heart defects, neural tube defects, and caudal regression. Gestational diabetes develops later, as placental hormones raise insulin resistance, so its effects fall mainly on fetal size and metabolism.
whyNot: Glucose passes from mother to embryo from the earliest weeks of pregnancy, so an embryo exposed to maternal hyperglycemia during organogenesis is affected.
The fetal pancreas begins secreting insulin only near the end of the first trimester, and it cannot shield the embryo from maternal glucose.
Maternal insulin does not cross the placenta, so it cannot protect the embryo directly.
Correct.

questions.stem: At her first visit, she reported stopping oral isotretinoin for acne 3 months before conception. Exposure to this drug during early pregnancy is most likely to cause which of the following patterns of defects?
options: Phocomelia and other limb reduction defects of the arms
Ebstein anomaly with downward tricuspid valve displacement
Craniofacial, heart, and central nervous system defects
Discolored teeth and impaired fetal long bone growth
approach: Recognize isotretinoin as a vitamin A derivative (a retinoid).
Recall that retinoic acid sets HOX gene patterns, especially in the hindbrain and neural crest.
Excess retinoid disrupts structures that depend on neural crest: the face and ears, the cardiac outflow tract, and the central nervous system.
questions.why: Isotretinoin and excess vitamin A act through retinoic acid receptors that control HOX gene expression along the body axis. Cranial neural crest cells are especially sensitive, so exposure causes small or absent ears, cleft palate and other facial defects, conotruncal heart defects, and brain malformations such as hydrocephalus. Because the drug is so teratogenic, people who can become pregnant must use reliable contraception during treatment and for 1 month afterward.
whyNot: Limb reduction defects such as phocomelia are the classic effect of thalidomide.
Ebstein anomaly is linked to lithium exposure in the first trimester.
Correct.
Tooth discoloration and impaired bone growth are linked to tetracyclines, which bind calcium in forming teeth and bone.

dx: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 (HSIL) in a woman exposed to DES in utero, with clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina as the related risk
case: A 56-year-old woman comes to the physician for follow-up of an abnormal cervical screening test. Her mother took diethylstilbestrol (DES) during the pregnancy with her. She smokes one pack of cigarettes daily. Cervical cytology shows a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, and testing is positive for HPV 16. Colposcopy shows a dense acetowhite lesion at the transformation zone and patches of red glandular mucosa in the upper vagina (vaginal adenosis). Cervical biopsy shows atypical, immature basaloid cells with a high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio occupying the full thickness of the squamous epithelium, with an intact basement membrane. Diagnosis: cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 (HSIL) in a woman exposed to DES in utero.

questions.stem: Eight years ago, a cervical biopsy showed koilocytes in the upper layers of the epithelium, with atypical immature cells limited to the lower third. Which of the following was the most likely classification of that earlier lesion?
options: CIN 3, high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion
CIN 2, high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion
Microinvasive squamous cell carcinoma
CIN 1, low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion
approach: Grade CIN by how much of the epithelial thickness is replaced by atypical immature cells.
Lower third is CIN 1, up to two thirds is CIN 2, and more than two thirds or full thickness is CIN 3.
Koilocytes in the upper layers reflect productive HPV infection, typical of low-grade lesions.
questions.why: High-risk HPV infects immature basal cells at the transformation zone. In CIN 1, atypical immature cells fill only the lower third of the epithelium, and the upper layers still mature and show koilocytes, cells with wrinkled nuclei and a clear halo around the nucleus from viral replication. CIN 1 is reported as a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL). As the atypical cells extend higher, the lesion becomes CIN 2 and then CIN 3, which together are called HSIL, as she has now.
whyNot: CIN 3 means atypical cells fill more than two thirds or the full thickness of the epithelium, as in her current biopsy.
CIN 2 means atypical cells extend into the middle third of the epithelium.
Microinvasive carcinoma requires tumor cells breaking through the basement membrane into the stroma.
Correct.

questions.stem: Lesional cells contain integrated HPV 16 DNA with high expression of the viral E7 protein. Which of the following effects of E7 most directly drives these cells into S phase?
options: Ubiquitin-mediated degradation of the p53 tumor suppressor
Promoter methylation that silences the p16 gene
Binding of Rb, which releases E2F transcription factors
Constitutive activation of RAS by a point mutation
approach: Separate the two HPV oncoproteins: E6 targets p53, and E7 targets Rb.
Rb normally holds E2F inactive until cyclin D-CDK4/6 phosphorylates it.
E7 binding frees E2F, so S-phase genes turn on without growth signals.
questions.why: Hypophosphorylated Rb binds E2F and blocks the G1 to S transition. High-risk HPV E7 binds Rb and releases E2F, which turns on the genes needed for DNA synthesis. E6 adds to this by tagging p53 for ubiquitin-mediated breakdown, so damaged cells neither arrest nor undergo apoptosis. Integration of viral DNA often disrupts the E2 regulatory gene and raises E6 and E7 expression. Because Rb is inactive, the cells overexpress p16, which pathologists use as a stain for high-risk HPV lesions.
whyNot: Degradation of p53 is the action of E6. It removes the DNA damage checkpoint and apoptosis.
In HPV lesions, p16 is strongly overexpressed because Rb is inactive, so silencing of p16 is not part of this pathway.
Correct.
RAS point mutations drive pancreatic, colon, and lung cancers. HPV oncoproteins do not act through RAS mutation.

topics: Rb and the G1 to S checkpoint

questions.stem: Her 11-year-old granddaughter is scheduled to receive the HPV vaccine. Which of the following best explains how this vaccine prevents infection?
options: Cytotoxic T cells that kill cells expressing E6 and E7
Neutralizing antibody to L1 virus-like particles
Mucosal IgA from replication of live attenuated virus
Antibodies to the E2 protein that block DNA integration
approach: Recall the vaccine content: the L1 major capsid protein, which self-assembles into virus-like particles with no viral DNA.
A noninfectious particle vaccine works mainly through antibodies.
High-titer neutralizing IgG reaches the genital mucosa and blocks virions before they infect basal cells.
questions.why: HPV vaccines contain the L1 capsid protein, which assembles into virus-like particles that look like the virus but carry no DNA. They induce high levels of neutralizing IgG that reaches the cervical mucosa and blocks infection of basal cells at sites of small injuries. The vaccine prevents new infection but does not clear an established one. Once infection occurs, cell-mediated immunity clears most HPV infections and low-grade lesions within about 1 to 2 years, which is why people with weak T cell immunity, such as those with HIV, have more persistent infection and more cervical cancer.
whyNot: T cell responses against E6 and E7 are the goal of therapeutic vaccines under study. Current preventive vaccines contain only L1 and do not target infected cells.
Correct.
HPV vaccines are not live. Virus-like particles contain no viral genome and cannot replicate.
E2 is a viral regulatory protein made inside infected cells and is not in the vaccine. Antibodies cannot reach it to block integration.

questions.stem: Which of the following malignancies can arise from the glandular epithelium of her vaginal adenosis?
options: Clear cell adenocarcinoma
Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma
Keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma
Malignant melanoma
approach: Link DES exposure in utero to vaginal adenosis: Mullerian glandular tissue left in the upper vagina.
Recall the malignancy that arises from this glandular tissue: clear cell adenocarcinoma.
Match the other vaginal tumors to their usual settings.
questions.why: DES was given to pregnant women in the United States from about 1940 to 1971. It disrupted the normal replacement of Mullerian glandular epithelium by squamous epithelium in the developing vagina, so many exposed daughters have vaginal adenosis, patches of glandular tissue in the upper vagina. A small fraction develop clear cell adenocarcinoma from this tissue, with peak risk in young adulthood. Vaginal squamous cell carcinoma is mostly HPV-related and arises from vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia in older women, and embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma is a grape-like mass in young girls.
whyNot: Correct.
Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides) is a grape-like, desmin-positive tumor of skeletal muscle origin in young girls. It is not related to DES.
Vaginal squamous cell carcinoma arises from squamous epithelium through HPV-related vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia, not from glandular adenosis.
Vaginal melanoma arises from melanocytes, is rare, and is not linked to DES.

dx: Invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix
case: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of bleeding after intercourse and a foul-smelling vaginal discharge for 4 months, and bilateral flank pain for 2 weeks. She has HIV infection and has not had cervical screening for 15 years. She has smoked for 30 years. Pelvic examination shows a friable, exophytic cervical mass that extends through both parametria to the pelvic sidewalls. Serum creatinine is 2.9 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1), urea nitrogen is 48 mg/dL (7 to 20), and calcium is 9.4 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5). CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 210/μL (500 to 1500). Ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis. Biopsy shows nests of keratinizing malignant squamous cells invading the cervical stroma. Diagnosis: invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains this patient's kidney dysfunction?
options: Ureteral compression by tumor in the parametria
Collapsing glomerulopathy from HIV infection
Hypercalcemia from tumor-secreted PTH-related peptide
Immune complex glomerulonephritis from tumor antigens
approach: Pair the high creatinine with bilateral hydronephrosis: this is postrenal (obstructive) kidney failure.
Cervical cancer spreads laterally into the parametria, where the ureters pass close to the cervix.
Her normal calcium and the imaging rule out the other causes.
questions.why: Invasive cervical carcinoma grows directly into the parametrial tissue beside the cervix. The ureters run through this tissue about 1 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix, so lateral spread can compress both of them. The result is bilateral hydronephrosis and postrenal kidney failure, a major cause of death in advanced cervical cancer. Bleeding after intercourse, from a friable tumor surface, is the classic early symptom.
whyNot: Correct.
HIV-associated nephropathy causes heavy proteinuria and large, echogenic kidneys. It does not cause hydronephrosis.
Squamous cell carcinomas can secrete PTH-related peptide, but her calcium is normal.
Immune complex glomerulonephritis causes hematuria and proteinuria with normal collecting systems. It does not explain hydronephrosis.

questions.stem: HPV genotyping of the tumor is performed. Which of the following patterns of infection most likely led to this cancer?
options: Transient infection with HPV 16
Persistent infection with HPV 16
Persistent infection with HPV 6
Persistent infection with HPV 11
approach: Separate high-risk types (16, 18, and others) from low-risk types (6 and 11), which cause warts.
Most HPV infections, even with high-risk types, clear within 1 to 2 years.
Cancer needs a high-risk type plus years of persistence, which her HIV infection and smoking promote.
questions.why: HPV 16 and 18 cause about 70% of cervical cancers. Most infections, including those with high-risk types, are cleared, and most CIN 1 regresses on its own. Cancer develops when a high-risk infection persists for years, which allows viral integration and steady E6 and E7 expression. Risk rises with early first intercourse, many sexual partners, smoking, and immunodeficiency such as HIV. Her lack of screening meant precursor lesions were never found and treated.
whyNot: A transient HPV 16 infection is cleared by the immune system and does not lead to cancer. Persistence is required.
Correct.
HPV 6 is a low-risk type that causes genital warts. Its E6 and E7 proteins bind p53 and Rb only weakly.
HPV 11, like HPV 6, is a low-risk type linked to genital warts and laryngeal papillomas, not cervical cancer.

questions.stem: Two weeks later, she has heavy bleeding from the tumor. If the uterine artery were ligated close to the cervix to control the bleeding, which of the following structures would be at greatest risk of injury?
options: Obturator nerve
Internal pudendal artery
Ureter
Inferior epigastric artery
approach: Recall the course of the uterine artery: from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, medially through the base of the broad ligament.
About 1 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix, it crosses above the ureter (water under the bridge).
A clamp placed here can catch the ureter.
questions.why: The uterine artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery and runs medially in the base of the broad ligament toward the cervix. Near the lateral fornix, about 1 to 2 cm from the cervix, it passes above the ureter, which is heading forward to the bladder. A clamp or ligature placed here can cut, crush, or tie off the ureter, so surgeons identify the ureter before ligating the uterine vessels. The same closeness explains why parametrial tumor obstructs the ureters.
whyNot: The obturator nerve runs along the lateral pelvic wall to the obturator canal, well away from the uterine artery near the cervix.
The internal pudendal artery leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen to supply the perineum. It does not lie beside the uterine artery at the cervix.
Correct.
The inferior epigastric artery arises from the external iliac artery and runs up the anterior abdominal wall.

questions.stem: The tumor arose at the cervical transformation zone. Which of the following epithelial changes at this site creates the cell population most vulnerable to HPV-driven neoplasia?
options: Glandular metaplasia of ectocervical squamous epithelium
Keratinization of the stratified squamous vaginal lining
Atrophy of nonkeratinized ectocervical epithelium
Squamous metaplasia of endocervical columnar epithelium
approach: Recall the two linings: simple columnar in the endocervix, nonkeratinized stratified squamous on the ectocervix and vagina.
In the acidic vagina after puberty, exposed columnar epithelium is replaced by squamous epithelium (squamous metaplasia).
Immature metaplastic cells in this zone are the main target of HPV.
questions.why: The endocervical canal is lined by mucus-secreting simple columnar epithelium, and the ectocervix and vagina by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. At puberty and in pregnancy, columnar epithelium is pushed out onto the ectocervix, where the acidic environment drives reserve cells to replace it with squamous epithelium. This area of ongoing squamous metaplasia is the transformation zone. Its immature, dividing metaplastic cells are especially vulnerable to high-risk HPV, so nearly all CIN and cervical carcinoma begin here.
whyNot: Glandular metaplasia of squamous epithelium is the reverse of what happens at the transformation zone.
The vaginal lining is normally nonkeratinized, and keratinization, as with prolapse, is not the source of cervical carcinoma.
Atrophy after menopause thins the squamous lining but does not create the immature metaplastic cells that HPV targets.
Correct.

dx: Uterine leiomyoma with heavy menstrual bleeding and iron deficiency anemia
case: A 36-year-old Black woman comes to the physician because of heavy menstrual bleeding with clots, pelvic pressure, and urinary frequency for 2 years. She and her partner have been trying to conceive for 18 months. Her cycles are regular, and a midluteal progesterone level confirms ovulation. Hysterosalpingography shows patent uterine tubes and a filling defect that distorts the uterine cavity. Pelvic examination shows an irregularly enlarged uterus the size of a 14-week gestation. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL (12.0 to 15.5), mean corpuscular volume is 72 fL (80 to 100), and ferritin is 6 ng/mL (15 to 150). Ultrasound shows several well-circumscribed hypoechoic myometrial masses, including a 3-cm submucosal mass. The larger masses are removed by myomectomy and are firm, white, and whorled on cut section. Diagnosis: uterine leiomyomas with heavy menstrual bleeding and iron deficiency anemia.

questions.stem: Several small intramural leiomyomas were left in place. Which of the following best predicts their course after menopause?
options: Dystrophic calcification followed by renewed rapid growth
Continued growth driven by rising gonadotropin levels
Shrinkage as ovarian estrogen production falls
Progression to diffuse adenomyosis of the myometrium
approach: Recall that leiomyomas are benign smooth muscle tumors whose growth depends on estrogen and progesterone.
Ovarian hormone production falls after menopause.
So fibroids usually stop growing and shrink.
questions.why: Leiomyomas are benign, well-circumscribed clonal tumors of myometrial smooth muscle with a whorled cut surface. Their cells carry more estrogen and progesterone receptors than normal myometrium, so they grow during the reproductive years, may enlarge in pregnancy, and usually shrink after menopause. They are more common, and appear earlier, in Black women. A uterine mass that grows after menopause should raise concern for a different tumor.
whyNot: Old fibroids often calcify after menopause, but calcified fibroids do not start growing again.
FSH and LH rise after menopause, but fibroid growth depends on estrogen and progesterone, not gonadotropins.
Correct.
Adenomyosis is endometrial tissue within the myometrium, a separate condition. Leiomyomas do not turn into it.

questions.stem: Her 63-year-old aunt was recently found to have a single, rapidly enlarging uterine mass 3 years after menopause. Which of the following histologic findings would most strongly indicate leiomyosarcoma rather than leiomyoma?
options: Tumor cell necrosis, marked atypia, and many mitoses
Whorled bundles of uniform spindle cells, rare mitoses
Hyaline degeneration with dystrophic calcification
Strong nuclear estrogen receptor and desmin staining
approach: Note the setting: one large, growing mass in a postmenopausal woman, unlike multiple fibroids that shrink.
Leiomyosarcoma is diagnosed by a combination of tumor cell necrosis, nuclear atypia, and a high mitotic rate.
It arises de novo and does not come from a preexisting fibroid.
questions.why: Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant smooth muscle tumor that usually arises de novo in perimenopausal or postmenopausal women. It typically forms a single, large, soft, poorly circumscribed mass with hemorrhage and necrosis. Under the microscope, the key features are coagulative tumor cell necrosis, marked nuclear atypia, and a high mitotic rate. Leiomyomas, by contrast, are usually multiple, firm, and well circumscribed, and they do not transform into leiomyosarcoma.
whyNot: Correct.
Whorled bundles of uniform spindle cells with rare mitoses describe an ordinary leiomyoma.
Hyaline degeneration and calcification are common benign changes in older leiomyomas.
Both leiomyomas and leiomyosarcomas are smooth muscle tumors, so both can stain for desmin and express estrogen receptors. Staining does not separate them.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains this patient's infertility?
options: Chronic anovulation from excess prolactin secretion
Tubal blockage from scarring after pelvic infection
Intrauterine adhesions after uterine curettage
Cavity distortion that impairs embryo implantation
approach: Classify infertility as ovulatory, tubal, or uterine.
She ovulates and her tubes are patent, so the cause is uterine.
A submucosal leiomyoma bulges into the cavity and disrupts the endometrium where the embryo must implant.
questions.why: Female infertility is grouped into ovulatory causes (PCOS, hyperprolactinemia, ovarian insufficiency), tubal causes (scarring from prior pelvic inflammatory disease), and uterine causes. This patient has regular ovulatory cycles and patent tubes, so the problem is uterine. A submucosal leiomyoma distorts the cavity and the overlying endometrium and interferes with implantation, and it also causes heavy bleeding. Removing it often improves fertility.
whyNot: Hyperprolactinemia suppresses GnRH and causes anovulation, but she has regular cycles with confirmed ovulation.
Tubal scarring from pelvic inflammatory disease blocks egg and sperm transport, but her tubes are patent.
Intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome) follow curettage and cause scant or absent menses, the opposite of her heavy bleeding.
Correct.

questions.stem: After myomectomy and iron replacement, she conceives. At 24 weeks' gestation, her hemoglobin has fallen to 10.8 g/dL. Which of the following combinations of findings would best indicate that this fall reflects normal plasma volume expansion rather than recurrent iron deficiency?
options: Reduced MCV and reduced ferritin
Normal MCV and normal ferritin
Reduced MCV and normal ferritin
Raised MCV and normal ferritin
approach: Recall that plasma volume rises about 40 to 50% in pregnancy, more than red cell mass, so hemoglobin falls by dilution.
Dilution lowers concentration but does not change red cell size or iron stores.
Iron deficiency lowers ferritin first and then produces small cells (low MCV).
questions.why: In pregnancy, plasma volume expands more than red cell mass, so hemoglobin concentration falls even when iron supply is adequate. This physiologic dilution leaves red cells normal in size and iron stores intact, so MCV and ferritin stay normal. Pregnancy needs roughly 1 g of extra iron for the larger maternal red cell mass, the fetus, and the placenta, so iron deficiency is common, especially after heavy menstrual losses like hers. Iron deficiency shows a low ferritin first and a low MCV as it advances.
whyNot: Low ferritin with small red cells is the pattern of iron deficiency.
Correct.
Small red cells with normal iron stores point to thalassemia trait or another cause, not dilution.
Large red cells with normal ferritin suggest folate or vitamin B12 deficiency.

dx: Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma arising in lichen sclerosus
case: A 74-year-old woman comes to the physician because of vulvar itching for many years and a painful sore on the vulva for 3 months. Physical examination shows thin, white, wrinkled, parchment-like plaques over the labia minora and perianal skin, with narrowing of the introitus. A 2-cm ulcerated, indurated mass is present on the right labium majus, and a firm 2-cm right inguinal lymph node is palpable. A biopsy of the mass shows invasive keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma with keratin pearls. Diagnosis: vulvar squamous cell carcinoma arising in lichen sclerosus.

questions.stem: Molecular studies are performed on the tumor and the adjacent epithelium. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Integrated HPV 16 DNA with diffuse p16 staining
TP53 mutation with no high-risk HPV DNA
Activating KRAS mutation in basal keratinocytes
Loss of mismatch repair protein MLH1
approach: Note the setting: an older woman with long-standing lichen sclerosus.
Vulvar carcinoma follows two pathways: HPV-related (younger women, usual VIN) and HPV-independent (older women, lichen sclerosus, differentiated VIN).
The HPV-independent pathway is driven by TP53 mutation.
questions.why: Most vulvar carcinomas in older women arise without HPV, in skin damaged by lichen sclerosus or other chronic inflammation. The precursor is differentiated VIN, which often carries TP53 mutations. HPV-related vulvar carcinoma occurs in younger women, arises from usual (HPV-associated) VIN, contains integrated high-risk HPV, and stains strongly for p16. HPV-independent tumors tend to have a worse prognosis.
whyNot: Integrated HPV 16 with strong p16 staining is the profile of HPV-related vulvar cancer, which affects younger women and arises from usual VIN.
Correct.
KRAS mutations drive pancreatic, colon, and lung cancers. They are not a defining step in either vulvar carcinoma pathway.
Mismatch repair loss is the pathway of Lynch syndrome tumors, such as colon and endometrial cancer, and is not the usual vulvar pathway.

questions.stem: Before the mass appeared, her physician had considered extramammary Paget disease as a cause of the itching. If a vulvar biopsy had shown large pale cells with mucin-rich cytoplasm scattered through the epidermis, which of the following would have been the most likely interpretation?
options: Ductal carcinoma cells spreading up from an invasive tumor
Malignant melanocytes confined to the epidermal basal layer
HPV-infected koilocytes of usual vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia
Intraepithelial adenocarcinoma, usually with no underlying tumor
approach: Recognize Paget cells: large pale cells with mucin, spread singly and in clusters through the epidermis.
In the breast, Paget disease of the nipple almost always signals an underlying carcinoma.
On the vulva, extramammary Paget disease is usually an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma with no underlying tumor.
questions.why: Extramammary Paget disease of the vulva is an adenocarcinoma confined to the epidermis. It presents as a red, scaly, itchy plaque. Paget disease of the nipple nearly always marks an underlying ductal carcinoma of the breast, but vulvar Paget disease usually has no underlying invasive tumor. Its mucin-containing Paget cells separate it from melanoma in situ and from vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia.
whyNot: Paget cells spreading from an underlying ductal carcinoma describe Paget disease of the nipple.
Melanoma in situ shows atypical melanocytes that lack mucin and stain for melanocytic markers such as S100.
Usual VIN shows immature basaloid cells with koilocytes, not large mucin-filled cells.
Correct.

questions.stem: A biopsy is taken from one of the white plaques. Which of the following histologic findings best accounts for their thin, parchment-like appearance?
options: Thinned epidermis over homogenized dermal collagen
Thickened epidermis with marked surface hyperkeratosis
Absent melanocytes in a normal epidermis
Noncaseating granulomas in the superficial dermis
approach: Match appearance to histology: thin, white, wrinkled skin means a thin epidermis.
The pale color and stiffness come from dense, hyalinized collagen in the upper dermis.
A band of lymphocytes often lies below this layer.
questions.why: Lichen sclerosus thins the epidermis, flattens the rete ridges, and replaces the upper dermis with pale, homogenized, fibrotic collagen above a band of lymphocytes. This produces white, parchment-like plaques that can shrink the labia and narrow the introitus. It occurs mostly in postmenopausal women, likely has an autoimmune basis, and carries a small increased risk of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, as in this patient.
whyNot: Correct.
A thickened epidermis with hyperkeratosis describes lichen simplex chronicus (squamous hyperplasia), caused by chronic rubbing and scratching.
Loss of melanocytes is vitiligo, which makes white skin of normal texture and thickness.
Noncaseating granulomas suggest Crohn disease or sarcoidosis involving the vulva.

questions.stem: The initial differential diagnosis of her vulvar mass included a large condyloma. Which of the following findings would identify condyloma acuminatum rather than condyloma latum?
options: Spirochetes seen on dark-field microscopy
Reactive serum rapid plasma reagin test
Koilocytes from HPV 6 or 11 infection
Flat, moist, broad-based papules
approach: Separate the two condylomas by cause: acuminatum from HPV, latum from secondary syphilis.
HPV 6 and 11 produce koilocytes in a raised, papillary wart.
Condyloma latum is full of treponemes and comes with positive syphilis serology.
questions.why: Condyloma acuminatum is a benign, raised, cauliflower-like wart caused mainly by low-risk HPV 6 and 11. Histology shows papillary squamous proliferation with koilocytes, cells with wrinkled nuclei and a clear halo around the nucleus. Condyloma latum is a flat, moist, highly infectious lesion of secondary syphilis that contains many spirochetes. High-risk HPV types, mainly 16 and 18, cause carcinomas of the cervix, vulva, vagina, penis, anus, and oropharynx.
whyNot: Spirochetes on dark-field microscopy point to condyloma latum of secondary syphilis.
A reactive RPR supports syphilis, which is the cause of condyloma latum.
Correct.
Flat, moist, broad-based papules describe condyloma latum. Condyloma acuminatum is raised and papillary.
